clue.text: His work was becoming, his correspondence with Gide possibly less so

definitions.text: His work was becoming, his correspondence with Gide possibly less so

parts.words: His work was becoming, his correspondence with Gide possibly less so
parts.note: the French novelist's first novel was titled Devenir! (Becoming); his long exchange of letters with Andre Gide was perhaps less becoming, in the sense of seemly

explanation.surface: A writer whose fiction was admirable but whose private letters to a famous friend were rather less flattering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Becoming' works twice: it names the novel Devenir! and then, with 'less so', means seemly.
explanation.definitionFit: Roger Martin du Gard, Nobel laureate, published Devenir! in 1909 and kept up a lifelong correspondence with Gide.

clue.text: Violet Hunt recorded her progress

parts.note: the novelist Violet Hunt wrote a book whose title is a young unmarried woman's Progress

explanation.surface: A novelist chronicled a young woman's advance through life.
explanation.walkthrough: Violet Hunt's 1894 novel was The Maiden's Progress; the clue pluralises the girl.
explanation.definitionFit: Young unmarried women, the heroines whose Progress Violet Hunt's novel title names.

clue.text: Only the lucid friend to aerial ——' "

definitions.text: Only the lucid friend to aerial

parts.words: Only the lucid friend to aerial
parts.note: a quotation about the moon, a clear friend only to those attacking from the air at night; the missing word completes the line

explanation.surface: A line of verse with its last word missing, about the moon helping night bombers.
explanation.definitionFit: Night bombers are attackers from the air, helped by a bright moon.

clue.text: Me Tarzan-type pronouncement by reluctant Roman supremo

definitions.text: Me Tarzan-type pronouncement by reluctant Roman supremo

parts.words: Me Tarzan-type pronouncement by reluctant Roman supremo
parts.note: like the jungle hero's blunt self-introduction, a pronoun followed by a name: the stammering emperor who never wanted the throne

explanation.surface: An unwilling emperor introduces himself in the clipped manner of a jungle hero.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Graves's novel title reads like 'Me Tarzan': pronoun plus name. The emperor was famously reluctant to rule.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Graves's novel narrated by the Roman emperor who was pushed onto the throne by the Praetorian Guard.

clue.text: Small subject of Par Lagerkvist

definitions.meaning: the Swedish Nobel laureate wrote a 1944 novel narrated by a malicious court midget

explanation.surface: A minor theme in the work of a Swedish writer.
explanation.definitionFit: Something stunted is tiny; Lagerkvist's novel Dvargen takes a tiny courtier as its narrator.

clue.text: Old ladies like she who finally got the needle in early play

definitions.meaning: an archaic rustic word for elderly women

definitions.text: like she who finally got the needle in early play
definitions.meaning: in the Tudor comedy Gammer Gurton's Needle, the old woman's lost needle is finally found

explanation.surface: Elderly women resembling the heroine of an early comedy who at last recovered her sewing needle.
explanation.walkthrough: Gammer Gurton's Needle is one of the earliest English comedies; 'got the needle' teases the slang sense of being annoyed.
explanation.definitionFit: Gammer is an old rural term for a grandmother or aged woman, as in the play's heroine.

clue.text: Our Edna might compose a formal poem

indicators.note: composing puts the letters of the name and pronoun into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone familiar called Edna could write a strictly structured verse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Might compose' rearranges OUREDNA.
explanation.definitionFit: A French verse form of fifteen lines with a refrain and only two rhymes.

clue.text: "The law is an ass", eg

parts.note: Dickens's Mr Bumble actually says the law is 'a ass', so the familiar version is an error of quotation

explanation.surface: A famous saying offered as an example.
explanation.walkthrough: In Oliver Twist Bumble says 'the law is a ass', so the usual form is wrong.
explanation.definitionFit: Getting a famous line slightly wrong when citing it is an error of quoting.

clue.text: Albert Otto Max Feige used a pseudonym, and a single one

definitions.text: Albert Otto Max Feige used a pseudonym, and a single one

parts.words: Albert Otto Max Feige used a pseudonym, and a single one
parts.note: Feige, thought to be the novelist B. Traven, published under a name with just one letter standing for a forename

explanation.surface: A biographical note on a mysterious German who wrote under a false name.
explanation.walkthrough: B. Traven's forename is reduced to one letter, B; 'a single one' is that letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A first letter standing for a name, as the B of B. Traven.

clue.text: "The Man i' the —— stuck with pins" (Nathaniel Lee)

definitions.text: "The Man i' the —— stuck with pins" (Nathaniel Lee)

parts.words: "The Man i' the —— stuck with pins" (Nathaniel Lee)
parts.note: the zodiac figure in old yearly calendars, a man pierced with lines to body parts, is the image the dramatist alludes to

explanation.surface: A line from a Restoration dramatist about a figure stuck full of pins.
explanation.walkthrough: Old annual calendars printed a 'zodiac man' with lines darting to each body part, like pins.
explanation.definitionFit: A yearly book of calendar, astronomical data and forecasts, which once printed the zodiac man.

clue.text: Rescue a celeb, somehow, from something like the Dreyfus affair

indicators.note: somehow says the letters of the three words get rearranged by some means

explanation.surface: Saving a celebrity in some way from a scandal resembling the Dreyfus case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Somehow' rearranges RESCUEACELEB.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dreyfus affair is the classic example of a notorious controversial trial that divides public opinion.

clue.text: Queue an awful solution for one producing portrait in the Métro

definitions.text: one producing portrait in the Métro

indicators.note: awful suggests the two words are badly mangled into a new order

explanation.surface: A dreadful queue as the answer for someone sketching a picture on the Paris underground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Awful' rearranges QUEUEAN. Raymond Queneau wrote Zazie dans le metro, a portrait of a girl in Paris.
explanation.definitionFit: Raymond Queneau wrote Zazie dans le metro, a comic portrait of a girl loose in Paris.

clue.text: A free UN somehow foreseen by American sailor poet?

indicators.note: somehow says the letters are rearranged in an unspecified way

explanation.surface: A free United Nations, oddly predicted by an American poet who went to sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Somehow' rearranges AFREEUN. Philip Freneau, 'Poet of the American Revolution', was also a sea captain.
explanation.definitionFit: Philip Freneau was a Revolutionary-era versifier who also captained merchant ships.

clue.text: Mary McCarthy's location of group

definitions.meaning: McCarthy's satirical novella about a utopian commune is titled after a refuge in a desert
a famous Manchester rock band of the 1990s

explanation.surface: The place where an American novelist set a collective.
explanation.definitionFit: McCarthy's novella The Oasis is set in a fertile desert refuge; the same name belongs to the Gallagher brothers' rock band.

clue.text: Act of "Rokesmith" (or of Boffin) is a burden to regret, possibly

parts.note: an impost is a tax or burden laid on someone

indicators.note: possibly says the letters of the regret word are reordered

explanation.surface: A character's deceit in a Dickens novel is described as a heavy load to be sorry about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Possibly' rearranges RUE to URE. In Our Mutual Friend John Harmon poses as Rokesmith and Boffin feigns miserliness.
explanation.definitionFit: Both characters in Our Mutual Friend practise a deception, pretending to be what they are not.

clue.text: Some pink elephant, as Macbeth's Porter might have seen — an apparition

indicators.note: some says only part of the run of words is wanted

explanation.surface: Part of a pink elephant, the sort of drunken vision Macbeth's tipsy Porter might have had: a ghost.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some' signals the letters hidden across elePHANT AS MAcbeth's; pink elephants are what drunks see, and the Porter is drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: A ghostly illusion or spectre, the kind of thing a drunk imagines.

clue.text: Lost Romanov in Anderson fairy tale?

definitions.text: Lost Romanov in Anderson fairy tale?

parts.words: Lost Romanov in Anderson fairy tale?
parts.note: Anna Anderson claimed to be the tsar's youngest daughter, a story many judged a fairy tale; the clue plays on Hans Andersen

explanation.surface: A missing Russian royal appears in a story by the Danish teller of tales.
explanation.walkthrough: Anna Anderson's claim to be the lost grand duchess was a fairy tale, DNA later showed; 'Anderson fairy tale' sounds like Hans Christian Andersen.
explanation.definitionFit: The tsar's youngest daughter, long rumoured to have survived the Bolshevik execution.

clue.text: A claw, say, for adviser to Augustus

indicators.note: say means the words are heard rather than read

parts.note: a claw is something that grips

explanation.surface: A talon, for instance, helping the first Roman emperor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' signals the spoken form: a gripper said in a non-rhotic accent.
explanation.definitionFit: Marcus Agrippa was Augustus's general, right-hand man and son-in-law.

clue.text: Occupation of Alfred Aloysius Horn

parts.note: this adventurer's African memoirs were published under the nickname Trader Horn, which names his business

explanation.surface: A question about what a particular man did for a living.
explanation.walkthrough: Alfred Aloysius Horn was known as Trader Horn from his 1927 bestselling memoir.
explanation.definitionFit: Buying and selling goods, the commerce that gave Trader Horn his nickname.

clue.text: Successful children's writer returns in golden limousine

indicators.note: returns says the hidden letters are read backwards
the clue word that says the letters sit inside the next words

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A prosperous author of books for the young comes back in a gilded car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' signals the hidden run across goldEN LIMousine, and 'returns' reads it backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A. A. Milne became wealthy through Winnie-the-Pooh.

clue.text: She and her brood were definitely not Janeites

definitions.text: She and her brood were definitely not Janeites

parts.words: She and her brood were definitely not Janeites
parts.note: Janeites are Austen devotees; here the play is on Jane Eyre, whose aunt and cousins hated her

explanation.surface: A mother and children who were no fans of Jane Austen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Janeites' looks like Austen fans, but the Jane is Jane Eyre, bullied at Gateshead by her aunt and cousins.
explanation.definitionFit: Jane Eyre's cruel aunt at Gateshead, whose children John, Eliza and Georgiana tormented the orphan.

clue.text: Sort of learned friend of Hero

indicators.note: sort of hints at a loose version of the word, its letters reordered

explanation.surface: A kind of legal companion to a protagonist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sort of' rearranges LEARNED; 'learned friend' is how British barristers address each other.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the youth swam the Hellespont nightly to visit his lover, the priestess Hero.

clue.text: Ordains, perhaps, the making of advances

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the letters of the word might take another order

explanation.surface: A church decree that may lead to progress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' rearranges ORDAINS.
explanation.definitionFit: Making gradual headway into territory, as in an attack or a market.

clue.text: Complete the puzzle by starting some other less vague exercise

indicators.note: by starting means taking the opening letter of each of the following words

explanation.surface: Finish the crossword by beginning another, clearer task.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By starting' takes the first letters of some other less vague exercise.
explanation.definitionFit: To work out every answer is to finish a crossword.

clue.text: How Forster's first Mrs Wilcox died — triggering the plot

definitions.text: How Forster's first Mrs Wilcox died — triggering the plot

parts.words: How Forster's first Mrs Wilcox died — triggering the plot
parts.note: Ruth Wilcox in Howards End leaves a note bequeathing the house to Margaret, so she dies having made a will of sorts

explanation.surface: A question about the death of a character in Howards End.
explanation.walkthrough: Ruth Wilcox's pencilled note leaving Howards End to Margaret Schlegel sets the novel in motion.
explanation.definitionFit: Having left a will, as Ruth Wilcox did with her note leaving the house to Margaret.

clue.text: "I hope you don't think me prone to any iteration of —s" (Congreve)

definitions.text: "I hope you don't think me prone to any iteration of —s" (Congreve)

parts.words: "I hope you don't think me prone to any iteration of —s" (Congreve)
parts.note: Millamant in The Way of the World says she is not eager to repeat weddings

explanation.surface: A line from a Restoration comedy about being reluctant to repeat something.
explanation.walkthrough: The line is Millamant's in The Way of the World; the plural is filled by adding s.
explanation.definitionFit: Relating to marriage; as a noun in plural, wedding ceremonies.

clue.text: English poet, perhaps, the last of the big ones?

definitions.meaning: Stephen, poet of the 1930s Auden group

definitions.text: the last of the big ones?
definitions.meaning: a big ___ is a lavish payer, so this word follows big

explanation.surface: An English poet might be the final lavish payer.
explanation.walkthrough: Stephen Spender was an English poet; 'big spender' is a lavish payer, so the answer is the last word of 'big ones'.
explanation.definitionFit: Stephen Spender was a 1930s poet; one who pays out freely is the second word of the phrase for a lavish customer.

clue.text: "Curst Common-sense, that imp o'hell, / Cam in wi' " (Robert Burns)

definitions.text: "Curst Common-sense, that imp o'hell, / Cam in wi' " (Robert Burns)

parts.words: "Curst Common-sense, that imp o'hell, / Cam in wi' " (Robert Burns)
parts.note: Burns's Scotch Drink-era verse names the heroine of a Scottish folk song as Common-sense's companion

explanation.surface: Lines from Burns about common sense arriving with a companion.
explanation.walkthrough: The companion is the heroine of a well-known Scottish folk song, quoted by Burns.
explanation.definitionFit: A traditional Scottish song heroine, named in Burns's lines as arriving with common sense.
